stem: The part of the eye that focuses light onto the retina is the __________.
solution: The eye lens focuses light to form an image on the retina.

stem: The light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye where the image forms is the __________.
solution: The retina is the light-sensitive layer where the image is formed.

stem: The image formed on the retina is __________.
solution: The eye lens forms a real, inverted image on the retina; the brain interprets it as upright.

stem: The coloured part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering is the __________.
solution: The iris adjusts the size of the pupil to control the light entering the eye.

stem: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to focus on near and distant objects is called __________.
solution: Accommodation is the eye lens changing its curvature (focal length) to focus at different distances.

stem: The muscles that change the curvature of the eye lens are the __________ muscles.
solution: The ciliary muscles adjust the curvature and focal length of the eye lens.

stem: The nearest point at which the eye can see an object clearly, called the near point, is about __________ for a normal eye.
solution: The least distance of distinct vision (near point) of a normal eye is about 25 cm.

stem: The farthest point up to which the eye can see clearly (the far point) of a normal eye is at __________.
solution: The far point of a normal eye is at infinity.

stem: The defect of vision in which a person cannot see distant objects clearly is called __________.
solution: Myopia (short-sightedness) is the inability to see distant objects clearly.

stem: Myopia is corrected using a __________ lens.
solution: A concave lens diverges rays so the image forms on the retina, correcting myopia.

stem: In myopia, the image of a distant object is formed __________ the retina.
solution: In myopia, the image forms in front of the retina, so distant objects appear blurred.

stem: The defect of vision in which a person cannot see nearby objects clearly is called __________.
solution: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is the inability to see nearby objects clearly.

stem: Hypermetropia is corrected using a __________ lens.
solution: A convex lens converges rays so the near image forms on the retina, correcting hypermetropia.

stem: In hypermetropia, the image of a nearby object is formed __________ the retina.
solution: In hypermetropia, the image forms behind the retina, so nearby objects appear blurred.

stem: The age-related defect in which the near point recedes, making it hard to see close objects, is called __________.
solution: Presbyopia is an age-related defect where the eye lens loses flexibility, making near vision difficult.

stem: A person having both myopia and hypermetropia may use __________ lenses.
solution: Bifocal lenses have a concave upper part (for distance) and a convex lower part (for near vision).

stem: The clouding of the eye lens in old age, causing blurred vision, is called __________.
solution: A cataract is the clouding of the eye lens, treated by surgical replacement with an artificial lens.

stem: The splitting of white light into its component colours by a prism is called __________.
solution: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven colours by a prism.

stem: The band of seven colours obtained after dispersion is called the __________.
solution: The spread of colours (VIBGYOR) is called the spectrum.

stem: In the spectrum, the colour that bends the most is __________.
solution: Violet light bends the most (has the shortest wavelength) and red the least.

stem: In the spectrum, the colour that bends the least is __________.
solution: Red light bends the least because it has the longest wavelength.

stem: A rainbow is formed by the __________ of sunlight by water droplets.
solution: A rainbow forms when raindrops refract, disperse and internally reflect sunlight into colours.

stem: The scattering of light by small particles depends on the __________ of the light.
solution: Scattering of light depends on wavelength; shorter wavelengths (blue) scatter more than longer ones (red).

stem: The sky appears blue during the day because __________.
options: blue light (shorter wavelength) is scattered more by air molecules
solution: Air molecules scatter shorter-wavelength blue light more than red, making the sky look blue.

stem: The Sun appears reddish at sunrise and sunset because __________.
options: blue light is scattered away, leaving red to reach us through the thick atmosphere
solution: At sunrise/sunset, light travels a longer path; most blue is scattered away, leaving the red to reach our eyes.

stem: The blinking of the eye when a bright light shines is an example of a __________ action.
solution: Blinking at bright light is a reflex action protecting the eye.

stem: The Tyndall effect is the __________ of light by colloidal particles.
solution: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal (fine) particles, making the beam visible.

stem: The colour of the clear sky at midday is __________, and at sunset it is __________.
solution: The sky is blue at midday (blue scattered most) and reddish at sunset (blue scattered away, red remaining).

stem: The eye is able to see objects in different levels of brightness because the __________ adjusts the pupil size.
solution: The iris widens or narrows the pupil to control the light entering the eye in bright or dim conditions.

stem: A prism deviates light, but does not disperse it into colours only if the light is __________.
solution: Monochromatic (single-colour) light is deviated but not dispersed, since it has only one wavelength.

stem: The image of a distant star appears to twinkle because of __________.
solution: Starlight is refracted by the changing atmosphere, making stars appear to twinkle.

stem: Planets do not twinkle as much as stars because they __________.
options: are closer and appear as extended sources, averaging out the fluctuations
solution: Planets are closer and appear as extended sources; the averaged light does not twinkle noticeably.

stem: The colour of an opaque object is the colour of light it __________.
solution: An opaque object appears the colour of light it reflects; the rest are absorbed.

stem: Which of the following corrects short-sightedness (myopia)?
options: A concave lens of suitable power
solution: A concave (diverging) lens of the correct power corrects myopia.

stem: Which of the following corrects long-sightedness (hypermetropia)?
options: A convex lens of suitable power
solution: A convex (converging) lens of the correct power corrects hypermetropia.

stem: The persistence of an image on the retina for about a __________ after the object is removed is called persistence of vision.
solution: Persistence of vision retains an image for about 1/16 of a second, which is the basis of cinema.

stem: The advanced sky colour (blue) is a result of __________ scattering by tiny molecules.
solution: Rayleigh scattering by small molecules scatters shorter (blue) wavelengths more, giving the blue sky.

stem: The cornea and eye lens together help in __________ light onto the retina.
solution: The cornea and lens refract (bend and focus) incoming light onto the retina.

stem: In a healthy eye, the far point at infinity allows a person to see __________.
solution: A normal eye's far point at infinity means distant objects can be seen clearly.

stem: Why does the sky appear dark to an astronaut in space?
options: There is no atmosphere to scatter sunlight
Light does not travel in space
solution: In space, there is no atmosphere to scatter sunlight, so the sky appears dark even during the day.

stem: The seven colours of the spectrum, in correct order, are __________.
options: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red
solution: The spectrum colours are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR).

stem: The eye lens is made of a __________ material that can change its shape.
solution: The eye lens is made of a flexible, jelly-like material, allowing it to change shape for accommodation.

stem: Danger and stop signals are made red because red light __________.
options: is scattered the least and is visible from the greatest distance
solution: Red light scatters least and travels the farthest through fog and air, so it is used for danger signals.

stem: Which of the following is a defect corrected by bifocal lenses?
options: Both myopia and hypermetropia in the same person
solution: Bifocal lenses correct both myopia (distance) and hypermetropia (near) in the same person.

stem: Why is white light dispersed but a rainbow shows a fixed order of colours?
options: Each colour has a different wavelength and refractive index, so they bend by different amounts
colours are added by the sky
solution: Different colours have different wavelengths and bend by different amounts on refraction, giving the fixed spectral order.

stem: The eye is able to adjust to see in bright sunlight and dim rooms because of the __________ and the retina's cells.
solution: The iris adjusts the pupil, and the retina's rods and cones let the eye see in dim and bright light.

stem: The refraction of light by the atmosphere causes the Sun to be visible __________ actual sunrise.
solution: Atmospheric refraction makes the Sun appear about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and after actual sunset.

stem: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected using a __________ lens.
solution: A concave (diverging) lens corrects myopia.

stem: The sky appears blue because blue light is __________ more by air molecules.
solution: Shorter-wavelength blue light is scattered more by air molecules, making the sky blue.

stem: The image formed on the retina of the eye is __________.
solution: The eye lens forms a real, inverted image on the retina, interpreted upright by the brain.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'The Human Eye and the Colourful World' is that:
options: the eye forms images by refraction and accommodation, has defects that lenses can correct, and phenomena like dispersion and scattering explain the colours of the sky and rainbow
the sky's colour has no explanation
solution: The chapter explains the working of the human eye, its defects and corrections, and atmospheric optical phenomena like dispersion, scattering, blue sky and red sunset.
